title: Jeremiah and the last days of Judah

intro.text: The prophets of Judah's last kings: Zephaniah in the days of Josiah; Jeremiah from Josiah's thirteenth year to the fall of Jerusalem and after; and Nahum, Habakkuk and Obadiah, whose books name no king.
When Nahum, Habakkuk and Obadiah spoke is a matter of views, set out with their holders on each page; they are placed here where many readers place them.

Jeremiah opposed four prophets by name: Hananiah, to whom he said “The LORD hath not sent thee”; Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, who “prophesy a lie unto you in my name”; and Shemaiah the Nehelamite, of whom the LORD said “I sent him not”. Their pages tell only what the text tells, in its words.

prophets.name: Zephaniah
prophets.title: Prophet in the days of Josiah (Zephaniah 1:1)
prophets.tagline: He proclaimed “the great day of the LORD” on Judah and the nations, and a humble remnant who would sing.

claim.text: “The word of the LORD which came unto Zephaniah … in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah.” The book records no meeting between them.

how.text: The book opens with the word of the LORD coming to him, and gives his line back four generations: son of Cushi, son of Gedaliah, son of Amariah, son of Hizkiah. Whether Hizkiah is King Hezekiah is an open question (below).
Much of the book speaks in the LORD's own voice (“I will utterly consume”, “I will search Jerusalem with candles”).

message.theme: The day of the LORD is near

claim.text: A day of wrath on all the land, when neither silver nor gold will deliver.

quotes.text: The great day of the LORD is near, it is near, and hasteth greatly
That day is a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress

claim.text: He names those who would be cut off: “the remnant of Baal”, the Chemarims, those who worship the host of heaven on the housetops, those who swear both by the LORD and by Malcham, and those who say the LORD will do neither good nor evil.

quotes.text: I will search Jerusalem with candles, and punish the men that are settled on their lees: that say in their heart, The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil.

claim.text: Before the day comes, the meek are told to seek righteousness and meekness: “it may be ye shall be hid”.

quotes.text: Seek ye the LORD, all ye meek of the earth, which have wrought his judgment; seek righteousness, seek meekness: it may be ye shall be hid in the day of the LORD’s anger.

claim.text: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod and Ekron; Moab and Ammon; the Ethiopians; and Assyria, whose city Nineveh would be made “a desolation, and dry like a wilderness”.
“The oppressing city” did not obey or receive correction: its princes, judges, prophets and priests are named one by one.
The LORD will turn to the peoples “a pure language”, leave “an afflicted and poor people” who trust in his name, and rejoice over Zion with singing.

quotes.text: The LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing.

quote.text: I will also stretch out mine hand upon Judah, and upon all the inhabitants of Jerusalem
Woe unto the inhabitants of the sea coast, the nation of the Cherethites!
Surely Moab shall be as Sodom, and the children of Ammon as Gomorrah
Ye Ethiopians also, ye shall be slain by my sword.
This is the rejoicing city that dwelt carelessly, that said in her heart, I am, and there is none beside me
Sing, O daughter of Zion; shout, O Israel; be glad and rejoice with all the heart, O daughter of Jerusalem.

claim.text: Three chapters, 53 verses, all given as the word of the LORD in Josiah's days: the day of the LORD on Judah, words against the nations around, and a turn from Jerusalem's sin to the remnant and a song.

outline.title: The day of the LORD on Judah
A pure language, a remnant, a song

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: The fish gate, Maktesh, the city searched with candles

scripture.text: Scripture says nothing of him beyond the first verse of his book.

questions.question: Is the “Hizkiah” of Zephaniah 1:1 King Hezekiah?

views.label: Yes, the king
views.holders: Ibn Ezra, as reported by the Jewish Encyclopedia (1904); Keil (1868); G. A. Smith (1898)

argument.text: Keil reasons that a line traced back four generations points to a well-known ancestor: Hezekiah “must have been a celebrated man, and that in all probability the king of that name is intended.” Smith: “Zephaniah's great-great-grandfather Hezekiah was in all probability the king.”

views.label: Possible but not certain
views.holders: A. B. Davidson (1896); S. R. Driver (1891)

argument.text: Davidson: “The royal descent of Zephaniah, though not certain, is supported by plausible grounds.” Driver only reports that “it is supposed by some” that the king is meant.

views.label: No
views.holders: Abravanel, as reported by the Jewish Encyclopedia (1904)

argument.text: The Jewish Encyclopedia says that Abravanel “rejected this identification.”

questions.question: Did Zephaniah speak before or after Josiah's reform?

views.label: Before the reform of Josiah's eighteenth year
views.holders: S. R. Driver (1891); A. B. Davidson (1896); G. A. Smith (1898)

argument.text: The worship he condemns (Zeph 1:4–6) was still standing. Driver: “it may be inferred with tolerable certainty that the period of Josiah's reign during which Zephaniah wrote was prior to the great reformation of his eighteenth year (B.C. 621)”. Smith dates chapter 1 “about 625 B.C.”

views.label: After it
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1868)

argument.text: Keil holds that the prophecy “in all probability was not uttered till after the completion of the repairs of the temple, and the celebration of the solemn passover in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign.”

notSaid: Scripture gives no call, no story and no death for Zephaniah; all it tells of him is in Zephaniah 1:1.
He is a different man from Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah, the priest of Zedekiah's day (Jer 21:1; 2 Kgs 25:18).
The New Testament does not quote Zephaniah by name.

prophets.name: Jeremiah
prophets.title: Prophet to Judah and the nations, from Josiah to the exile
prophets.tagline: The word came to him from Josiah's thirteenth year until Jerusalem fell; his last recorded words were spoken in Egypt.

claim.text: The word first came to Jeremiah “in the thirteenth year of his reign” (Jer 1:2), and one saying is dated “in the days of Josiah the king” (Jer 3:6). Chronicles says that “Jeremiah lamented for Josiah” when he died (2 Chr 35:25). Later Jeremiah held Josiah up to his son as a king who “judged the cause of the poor and needy”.

quote.text: He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well with him: was not this to know me? saith the LORD.

claim.text: Jeremiah calls him “Shallum the son of Josiah king of Judah, which reigned instead of Josiah his father”, and told Judah to weep not for the dead king but for the son taken away, who would die where he was led captive. Kings calls the son who followed Josiah Jehoahaz.

quote.text: weep sore for him that goeth away: for he shall return no more, nor see his native country

claim.text: At the beginning of his reign Jeremiah preached in the temple court that the house would be made “like Shiloh”, and was nearly put to death; the king killed the prophet Urijah, who spoke the same words. Jeremiah's scroll, written in the king's fourth year, was read to him in his fifth and burned, and the king ordered Jeremiah and Baruch taken, “but the LORD hid them”. Jeremiah said he would have “the burial of an ass”.

quote.text: He shall have none to sit upon the throne of David: and his dead body shall be cast out in the day to the heat, and in the night to the frost.

claim.text: Jeremiah calls him Coniah and Jeconiah. He said that though Coniah were “the signet upon my right hand”, the LORD would pluck him off and cast him into another country. Jeremiah's vision of the figs came after Jeconiah was carried to Babylon, and Hananiah promised his return within two years. The book ends with his release from prison in Babylon.

quote.text: Write ye this man childless, a man that shall not prosper in his days: for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah.

claim.text: Zedekiah sent to Jeremiah to enquire of the LORD and to ask his prayers, shut him up in the court of the prison, gave him up to the princes, and asked him in secret, “Is there any word from the LORD?” Jeremiah told him to go out to the king of Babylon's princes and live. Chronicles says the king “humbled not himself before Jeremiah the prophet speaking from the mouth of the LORD”.

quote.text: If thou wilt assuredly go forth unto the king of Babylon’s princes, then thy soul shall live, and this city shall not be burned with fire

claim.text: Jeremiah calls the king of Babylon the LORD's “servant”, to whom the LORD had given the lands. When Jerusalem fell, Nebuchadrezzar gave charge concerning Jeremiah to Nebuzar-adan the captain of the guard.

quote.text: Take him, and look well to him, and do him no harm; but do unto him even as he shall say unto thee.

claim.text: Two passages tell how Jeremiah came to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had made governor. In one the Babylonian princes take him out of the court of the prison and commit him to Gedaliah; in the other Nebuzar-adan lets him go at Ramah, and he goes to Gedaliah at Mizpah and dwells with him among the people left in the land (see the question below).

quote.text: Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations.

claim.text: The word came “in the thirteenth year” of Josiah. Jeremiah answered, “Ah, Lord GOD! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child.” The LORD told him not to say so, nor to be afraid of their faces, touched his mouth and said, “Behold, I have put my words in thy mouth,” and set him “over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant.”

quote.text: For, behold, I have made thee this day a defenced city, and an iron pillar, and brasen walls against the whole land

claim.text: The call goes on with two things the LORD showed him, a rod of an almond tree and a seething pot facing from the north, and a charge: “Thou therefore gird up thy loins, and arise, and speak unto them all that I command thee.” Kings, princes, priests and people would fight against him, “but they shall not prevail against thee”.

how.text: Many sections of the book open by saying that the word came to Jeremiah from the LORD (Jer 7:1; 11:1; 18:1; 21:1; 30:1; 32:1; 34:1; 35:1; 40:1).
Sometimes the word came as something to look at, with the question “What seest thou?”: the almond rod, the seething pot and two baskets of figs.

Often he was told to do something and then say what it meant, sometimes before witnesses: hide a girdle, break a bottle, wear a yoke, buy a field, hide stones (see Signs). His own life was made a sign: “Thou shalt not take thee a wife, neither shalt thou have sons or daughters in this place.”

The words were written down. Baruch wrote “from the mouth of Jeremiah” on a roll of a book; asked how, Baruch said, “He pronounced all these words unto me with his mouth, and I wrote them with ink in the book.” Jeremiah was also told “Write thee all the words that I have spoken unto thee in a book”, sent a letter to the captives in Babylon, and wrote in a book the evil to come on Babylon.
He could not always answer at once. When Hananiah broke the yoke, “the prophet Jeremiah went his way” until the word came; when the remnant asked him to pray, the word came “after ten days”.
Three times he was told not to pray for the people: “Therefore pray not thou for this people”. Yet he prayed to the LORD after buying the field, and promised the remnant he would pray for them.

He says he tried to keep silent and could not: “his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay.” And: “Thy words were found, and I did eat them”.

claim.text: The people had turned from the LORD to other gods, like a people who leave a spring for cracked water-tanks; the LORD calls to backsliding Israel, “Return, thou backsliding Israel”, and tells the men of Judah to “take away the foreskins of your heart”.

quotes.text: For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.

claim.text: At the gate of the LORD's house he warned that the temple would not save a people who stole, murdered and followed Baal; the LORD would do to it as he had done to Shiloh. Jesus later spoke of the temple as made “a den of thieves” (see The book).

quotes.text: Trust ye not in lying words, saying, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, are these.
Is this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes?

message.theme: Amend your ways: justice for the weak

claim.text: The call to “amend your ways and your doings” is spelled out: judge fairly, do not oppress the stranger, the fatherless and the widow, shed no innocent blood, pay workers their wages, keep the sabbath, and let the Hebrew servants go free as the covenant said. Under Zedekiah the people set them free, then took them back.

quotes.text: Woe unto him that buildeth his house by unrighteousness, and his chambers by wrong; that useth his neighbour’s service without wages, and giveth him not for his work

claim.text: The book speaks of the heart again and again: the people walk in “the imagination of their heart”, the LORD searches it, and the trouble lies there.

quotes.text: The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD, and whose hope the LORD is.

message.theme: Evil out of the north: serve the king of Babylon and live

claim.text: From the first vision the judgment comes “out of the north”. Later it is named: Nebuchadrezzar, the LORD's servant. Jeremiah told Judah and the nations to put their necks under his yoke and live, and told the people in the siege that whoever went out to the Chaldeans would live.

quotes.text: Behold, I set before you the way of life, and the way of death.
Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people, and live.

claim.text: Other prophets promised peace. Jeremiah said the LORD had not sent them: they spoke “a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD”.

quotes.text: They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.
I have not sent these prophets, yet they ran: I have not spoken to them, yet they prophesied.
Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?

claim.text: The nations would serve the king of Babylon seventy years; then the LORD would punish Babylon and bring the captives back. Meanwhile the captives were to build houses, plant gardens, marry, and pray for the city they were taken to. Daniel later “understood by books the number of the years” of this word to Jeremiah.

quotes.text: these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years
That after seventy years be accomplished at Babylon I will visit you, and perform my good word toward you, in causing you to return to this place.
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.

claim.text: In the chapters of comfort (30–33) the LORD promises to bring back the captivity of Israel and Judah, to raise up for David “a righteous Branch”, and to make “a new covenant”: not like the one broken after Egypt, but written in the heart, with sins forgiven. Hebrews quotes it in full (Heb 8:8–12) and in part again (10:16–17).

quotes.text: Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah
I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.
for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.

claim.text: He was ordained “a prophet unto the nations”. He made the nations drink the cup of the LORD's fury, and the book gathers his words against Egypt, the Philistines, Moab, Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, Elam and, last and longest, Babylon.

quotes.text: Take the wine cup of this fury at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send thee, to drink it.

message.theme: The prophet's own grief and complaint

claim.text: The book gives his own words to God: grief for his people, complaint at his enemies, the question why the wicked prosper, and a curse on the day he was born.

quotes.text: Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!
Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there?
Cursed be the day wherein I was born

quote.text: The LORD hath not called thy name Pashur, but Magor-missabib.

claim.text: Said the morning after Pashur had him beaten and put in the stocks. Pashur and his house would go to Babylon and die there, with the friends to whom he had “prophesied lies”.

quote.text: Hear now, Hananiah; The LORD hath not sent thee; but thou makest this people to trust in a lie.
Thou hast burned this roll

claim.text: Sent after the king burned the scroll: none of his line would sit on David's throne, and his body would be cast out.

quote.text: O earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the LORD.
Thou shalt not die by the sword: But thou shalt die in peace

claim.text: In the same message: the city would be burned, and Zedekiah would see the king of Babylon's eyes and go to Babylon.

quote.text: Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them

claim.text: A letter sent from Jerusalem by the hand of Elasah and Gemariah.

quote.text: Jonadab the son of Rechab shall not want a man to stand before me for ever.
And seekest thou great things for thyself? seek them not

claim.text: Baruch had said, “Woe is me now!” The answer: his life would be given him “for a prey in all places whither thou goest”.

quote.text: thou shalt not fall by the sword, but thy life shall be for a prey unto thee: because thou hast put thy trust in me

words.to: The remnant at Geruth Chimham, by Bethlehem

quote.text: Go ye not into Egypt

claim.text: The answer they had asked him to seek, given after ten days: stay in the land and be built up; go to Egypt and die there by sword, famine and pestilence.

quote.text: all the remnant of Judah, that are gone into the land of Egypt to sojourn there, shall know whose words shall stand, mine, or theirs.

claim.text: Spoken to the Jews at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Noph and Pathros, who answered that they would go on burning incense to the queen of heaven.

quote.text: Behold, I will give Pharaoh-hophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies

claim.text: Given as “a sign unto you” to the Jews in Egypt.

quote.text: Against Egypt, against the army of Pharaoh-necho king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates in Carchemish
The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet against the Philistines, before that Pharaoh smote Gaza.
Woe unto Nebo! for it is spoiled
Hath Israel no sons? hath he no heir?
Is wisdom no more in Teman? is counsel perished from the prudent?
Concerning Damascus. Hamath is confounded, and Arpad: for they have heard evil tidings

words.to: Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor

quote.text: Arise ye, go up to Kedar, and spoil the men of the east.
The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet against Elam in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah
Thus shall Babylon sink, and shall not rise from the evil that I will bring upon her
I will bring evil upon the men of Anathoth, even the year of their visitation.

claim.text: His own townsmen had said, “Prophesy not in the name of the LORD, that thou die not by our hand”.

signs.label: A rod of an almond tree

claim.text: “I see a rod of an almond tree.” The LORD answered, “Thou hast well seen: for I will hasten my word to perform it.”

signs.label: A seething pot from the north

claim.text: A boiling pot facing from the north: “Out of the north an evil shall break forth upon all the inhabitants of the land.”

He was told to get a linen girdle, wear it without putting it in water, then go to Euphrates and hide it “in a hole of the rock”. After many days he dug it up: “the girdle was marred, it was profitable for nothing.” So, the LORD said, he would mar the pride of Judah and Jerusalem, a people he had made to cleave to him as a girdle cleaves to a man.

signs.label: No wife, no mourning, no feasting

claim.text: He was not to marry or have children “in this place”, not to enter a house of mourning nor a house of feasting, because the LORD would take away mourning for the dead and “the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride”.
He went down to the potter's house and watched a vessel marred on the wheel and made again: “as the clay is in the potter’s hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel.”

He was told to get a potter's earthen bottle, take elders of the people and of the priests to the valley of the son of Hinnom, speak the word there, and break the bottle in their sight: “Even so will I break this people and this city, as one breaketh a potter’s vessel, that cannot be made whole again.” Then “came Jeremiah from Tophet”, spoke in the temple court, and Pashur put him in the stocks. The text gives the command; it does not narrate the breaking.

After Jeconiah was carried away, the LORD showed him a basket of very good figs and a basket of figs too bad to eat: the good were the captives in Babylon, whom he would bring back; the bad were Zedekiah, his princes and those left in the land or living in Egypt.
“Then took I the cup at the LORD’s hand, and made all the nations to drink, unto whom the LORD had sent me”, beginning with Jerusalem. The text does not say how this was done.

He was told to make bonds and yokes, put them on his neck, and send them to the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Zidon by their envoys in Jerusalem: serve the king of Babylon and live. He wore one, for Hananiah took the yoke from his neck and broke it; the LORD answered, “Thou hast broken the yokes of wood; but thou shalt make for them yokes of iron.”

He brought the Rechabites into a chamber of the temple and set wine before them. They refused, because their father Jonadab had commanded it; their obedience was set against Judah's refusal to hear the LORD.

Shut in the court of the prison during the siege, he bought his cousin Hanameel's field at Anathoth for seventeen shekels of silver, sealed the deeds before witnesses and had Baruch put them in an earthen vessel: “Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land.”

In Egypt the LORD told him to take great stones and hide them in the clay in the brickkiln at the entry of Pharaoh's house in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah, and to say that Nebuchadrezzar would set his throne on them and smite Egypt. The text gives the command and the words; it does not go on to tell the act.

signs.label: A book sunk in the Euphrates

claim.text: Jeremiah wrote the evil to come on Babylon in a book and told Seraiah, going to Babylon with Zedekiah, to read it there, bind a stone to it and cast it into the Euphrates: “Thus shall Babylon sink”. The text gives the charge; it does not say that Seraiah did it.

word.text: “Behold, Hanameel the son of Shallum thine uncle shall come unto thee, saying, Buy thee my field that is in Anathoth”.

reported.text: “So Hanameel mine uncle’s son came to me in the court of the prison according to the word of the LORD … Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD.”

word.text: To Hananiah: “this year thou shalt die, because thou hast taught rebellion against the LORD.”

reported.text: “So Hananiah the prophet died the same year in the seventh month.”

word.text: The city would be given into the hand of the king of Babylon and burned.

reported.text: During the siege Jeremiah prayed, “what thou hast spoken is come to pass; and, behold, thou seest it.” After the fall Nebuzar-adan, captain of the guard, told him, “Now the LORD hath brought it, and done according as he hath said”.

word.text: Seventy years of serving Babylon, then the return.

reported.text: Chronicles says the land lay desolate “To fulfil the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah … to fulfil threescore and ten years”, and that Cyrus's decree came “that the word of the LORD spoken by the mouth of Jeremiah might be accomplished”; Ezra opens with the same words. How the seventy years are counted is an open question (below).

word.text: “A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not.”

reported.text: After Herod killed the children of Bethlehem, Matthew writes: “Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet”.

word.text: Matthew quotes words about “thirty pieces of silver” and “the potter’s field” as “spoken by Jeremy the prophet”. The nearest wording in the Old Testament is in Zechariah 11:12–13; Jeremiah tells of a potter's house and of buying a field (Jer 18; 32). See the open question below.

reported.text: When the priests bought the potter's field with the money Judas returned, Matthew writes: “Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet”.

claim.text: Fifty-two chapters: dated and undated sayings, stories about the prophet told in the third person, letters, and words against the nations. It is not in time order (the fourth year of Jehoiakim comes in chapters 25, 36 and 45; Zedekiah's reign in 21, 24, 27–29, 32–34 and 37–39). It tells of a scroll Baruch wrote at Jeremiah's dictation, burned by the king and written again with “many like words” added; and its last chapter retells the fall of Jerusalem after the words “Thus far are the words of Jeremiah”.

Words to the kings and the prophets; the two baskets of figs
Seventy years, and the cup for the nations
Trial in the temple, the yokes, Hananiah, the letter to the captives
The book of comfort: return, new covenant, the field
Zedekiah's broken covenant, the Rechabites, the burned scroll, the prison
The fall, Gedaliah, the flight to Egypt, words to Baruch

quotedInNT.note: “Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet”.
“It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer” is Isaiah 56:7; “a den of thieves” answers Jeremiah's “den of robbers”.
“As it is written”: a short form of Jeremiah 9:23–24.
The same short form, without “it is written”.

The new covenant, quoted in full. Where the King James Old Testament has “although I was an husband unto them”, Hebrews 8:9 has “I regarded them not”, as the Greek does (“I disregarded them”, Brenton 1844, Greek chapter 38:32).
Part of it again, after the words “the Holy Ghost also is a witness to us” (Hebrews 10:15).

claim.text: Five poems over fallen Jerusalem. Chapters 1, 2, 4 and 5 have twenty-two verses each, and chapter 3 sixty-six (three times twenty-two). The poems do not name their author; the King James title, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, follows tradition (see the question). Chronicles says “Jeremiah lamented for Josiah” and that laments “are written in the lamentations”.

outline.title: “I am the man that hath seen affliction”

claim.text: His scribe. Baruch kept the deeds of the field, wrote the scroll at his mouth and read it in the temple, hid with him from the king, wrote it again, was accused of setting him against the remnant, and was taken with him to Egypt.
“A quiet prince”, who went to Babylon with Zedekiah in his fourth year; Jeremiah gave him the book against Babylon to read there.
A eunuch in the king's house. When Jeremiah was sinking in the mire of the dungeon, he went to the king, and with thirty men drew him up with cords, padding them with old rags under his arms.
“The hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah, that they should not give him into the hand of the people to put him to death.”

person.name: The princes and elders at his trial

claim.text: When the priests and prophets said “This man is worthy to die”, the princes and people answered “This man is not worthy to die”, and elders recalled that Hezekiah had not put Micah the Morasthite to death.
A man who “prophesied in the name of the LORD … according to all the words of Jeremiah”. He fled to Egypt; Jehoiakim had him brought back and killed him with the sword.
Son of Jeremiah's uncle Shallum; he sold Jeremiah the field at Anathoth.
Princes who begged Jehoiakim not to burn the roll; “he would not hear them”.
Priest and “chief governor in the house of the LORD”, who smote him and put him in the stocks.

person.name: Pashur son of Melchiah and the princes

claim.text: Pashur was sent by Zedekiah to enquire of Jeremiah; later he and other princes asked the king to put Jeremiah to death, and they let him down into the dungeon of Malchiah.

person.name: Irijah the captain of the ward

claim.text: Seized Jeremiah in the gate of Benjamin: “Thou fallest away to the Chaldeans.” Jeremiah answered, “It is false”.

person.name: Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest

claim.text: Sent twice by Zedekiah to Jeremiah. When Shemaiah wrote asking why he had not reproved Jeremiah, “Zephaniah the priest read this letter in the ears of Jeremiah the prophet.”
The prophets he opposed by name; each has a page of his own in this group.

person.name: Nebuzar-adan the captain of the guard

claim.text: Loosed him from his chains at Ramah and gave him the choice of Babylon or the land, with food and a reward.

scripture.text: He was taken to Egypt against his word with the remnant and Baruch, and came to Tahpanhes.
His last recorded words are to the Jews in Egypt, at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Noph and Pathros.
Scripture does not say where, when or how he died. The book closes his words with “Thus far are the words of Jeremiah” (51:64) and adds the fall of Jerusalem and Jehoiachin's release (52).

Later Scripture remembers him: Daniel “understood by books” the seventy years of “the word of the LORD” to Jeremiah; Chronicles and Ezra name him at Cyrus's decree; and when Jesus asked who people said he was, some said “Jeremias”.

tradition.text: “Jeremiah [Ermya] was from Anathoth, of the tribe of the Levites; and in Pitos and Egypt he was stoned by the people of the Jews, and there he died, and was buried.” The Egyptians honoured him.
tradition.who: The Lives of the Prophets, ascribed to Epiphanius of Cyprus (a Syriac copy, translated by I. H. Hall, 1887)
tradition.when: The ascription to Epiphanius (bishop from AD 367) is doubted (Davidson 1896); its date is not settled here

tradition.text: “David is persecuted; Elias put to flight; Jeremias stoned; Esaias cut asunder”. No place is named. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) calls this the first mention of the tradition that he was stoned in Egypt.
“Jeremiah announced the captivity and was stoned by the people.” No place is named.
tradition.when: late 4th century (he writes that “about four hundred years have passed since the preaching of Christ”)

tradition.text: In this book the people of Jerusalem stone Jeremiah after the return from Babylon. Harris notes that later church tradition put the stoning “at Tahpanhes in Egypt, and not, as the Jerusalem tradition and the Christian Baruch say, in Jerusalem.”
tradition.who: The Rest of the Words of Baruch (4 Baruch), edited by J. Rendel Harris (1889)

tradition.when: Mishnah age (by about AD 200) if by Rabbi Jose ben Halafta, to whom the Talmud ascribes it (Jewish Encyclopedia, 1905)

tradition.text: Josephus tells of Johanan carrying “Jeremiah and Baruch” into Egypt and of Nebuchadnezzar later taking the Jews in Egypt captive to Babylon. He says nothing of how Jeremiah died.

questions.question: Why are the Hebrew and the Greek books of Jeremiah different?

views.label: The Greek keeps an earlier, shorter Hebrew text
views.holders: J. D. Michaelis and Movers (as reported by Keil, 1874); G. C. Workman (1889); A. W. Streane (1896); M. Faulhaber (Catholic Encyclopedia, 1910); E. Tov (facts only, as reviewed by R. S. Hess, 2017)

argument.text: The Greek (Septuagint) lacks about an eighth of the Hebrew wording, and puts the words against the nations (Hebrew chapters 46–51) after 25:13, in another order. Workman: “The Septuagint presents not only a purer and an earlier, but also a superior, form of the book.” Streane: the “omissions” exist “in consequence of its nearer approximation to the original form of the Hebrew text”. Since then Hebrew fragments of Jeremiah have been found at Qumran; reviewing Tov, Hess (2017) writes that the earlier short editions “may be found in the Septuagint and in 4QJerb and 4QJerd.”

views.label: The Greek translator shortened and rearranged it
views.holders: K. H. Graf (1862); C. F. Keil (1874); Easton's Bible Dictionary (1897)

argument.text: Keil reports Graf's count, “about 2700 words of the Masoretic text, or somewhere about the eighth part of the whole”, and blames “the translator's arbitrariness, carelessness, and want of apprehension.” Graf: “it can hardly be called a translation”.

views.label: Weigh each reading; on the whole the Hebrew
views.holders: S. R. Driver (1891)

argument.text: Driver: “The number of words in the Hebrew text not represented in the LXX has been calculated at 2700, or one-eighth of the entire book.” The claims of each text “have been greatly exaggerated by their respective advocates; on the whole, the Massoretic text deserves the preference; but it is impossible to uphold the unconditional superiority of either.”

questions.question: How are the seventy years counted?

views.label: From Jehoiakim's fourth year to Cyrus
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1874, and on Daniel, 1872); Ellicott's Commentary

argument.text: Keil holds the seventy years are “not a so-called round number, but a chronologically exact prediction”: “From the 4th year of Jehoiakim, i.e., 606 b.c., till the 1st year of the sole supremacy of Cyrus over Babylon, i.e., 536 b.c., gives a period of 70 years.” Jeremiah 25:1 dates the prophecy to that fourth year; Ezra 1:1 and 2 Chronicles 36:22 tie its end to Cyrus.

views.label: From the destruction of the temple to its rebuilding
views.holders: Ewald (as reported by Keil); the Pulpit Commentary, as one of two reckonings

argument.text: In the second year of Darius an angel asks how long the LORD's indignation will last on Jerusalem, “these threescore and ten years” (Zech 1:7, 12). The Pulpit Commentary: “the second dates from the final destruction of Jerusalem, B.C. 588, unto the second year of Darius, B.C. 519”.

views.label: A round number
views.holders: A. W. Streane (1881); the Pulpit Commentary on Jeremiah; A. S. Peake (1910)

argument.text: Streane: “The Jewish love for round numbers and especially for one so significant in symbolism, as having for its elements seven and ten, would cause the number seventy … to stand for any number not differing by much from that amount.” Peake: “More probably we must regard it as a round number”, as Jeremiah 27:7 speaks of Nebuchadnezzar, “his son, and his son's son.”

questions.question: Why does Matthew 27:9 name Jeremiah for words close to Zechariah 11:12–13?

views.label: A slip of memory that the Spirit allowed to stand
views.holders: Augustine, Harmony of the Gospels 3.7.29–31 (about AD 400)

argument.text: Augustine rejects the defence that some copies lack the name, since “a majority of codices contain the name of Jeremiah”. He suggests “the word Jeremiah occurred to his mind … instead of Zechariah”, and that it is “a most consistent thing for us to credit Jeremiah with a sentence originally spoken by Zechariah”, pointing also to Jeremiah's purchase of a field.

views.label: Matthew quoted a Hebrew writing ascribed to Jeremiah
views.holders: Jerome, as reported by John Gill and Adam Clarke

argument.text: Gill: “Jerom affirms, that in an Hebrew volume, being an apocryphal work of Jeremy, which was shown him by one of the Nazarene sect, he read these words verbatim”. Clarke adds his own doubt that the words were “inserted there only to countenance the quotation here.”

views.label: “Jeremiah” names the whole book of the prophets
views.holders: John Lightfoot (1658), as quoted by Jamieson, Fausset and Brown (1871); M. B. Riddle (1888)

argument.text: The Talmud gives the order of the prophets as “Jehoshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah, and the Twelve Prophets” (Baba Bathra 14b). Lightfoot: Matthew “only cites the words of the volume of the prophets under his name who stood first in the volume of the prophets.” Ellicott's Commentary calls this “possible” but doubts it.

questions.question: Were the yokes of Jeremiah 27 made under Jehoiakim or under Zedekiah?

views.label: “Jehoiakim” in 27:1 is a copyist's slip for Zedekiah
views.holders: the Syriac version; Ellicott's Commentary; the Cambridge Bible (Streane)

argument.text: Verse 3 names “Zedekiah king of Judah”, verse 12 is spoken to him, and 28:1 dates Hananiah's answer to Zedekiah's reign. Ellicott: the mention of Zedekiah “shows that the Hebrew text has here perpetuated an error.” The Greek Septuagint has no verse 1 at all (Brenton, Greek chapter 34).

views.label: Made under Jehoiakim, sent under Zedekiah
views.holders: John Gill (1748–63)

argument.text: Gill favours the view that the prophet made the yokes in the beginning of Jehoiakim's reign and put one on his neck, while the rest were sent to the envoys of the nations in Zedekiah's time.

views.label: “The beginning” of Zedekiah's reign, read broadly
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1874)

argument.text: Keil reads the heading as corrected to Zedekiah and argues that “the idea of beginning is relative”, covering his early years of submission, so that it fits “the fourth year” of 28:1.

questions.question: How was Jeremiah set free when Jerusalem fell?

views.label: Two stages: freed from the prison court, then caught up among the captives
views.holders: Ellicott's Commentary; the Pulpit Commentary

argument.text: Jeremiah 39:11–14 has the Babylonian princes take him out of the court of the prison and commit him to Gedaliah; 40:1–6 has Nebuzar-adan loose him from chains at Ramah. Ellicott: “in the confusion at the burning of the city he seems to have been led away in chains with the other captives, and not till he reached Ramah to have gained full liberty.”

views.label: 39:11–13 is a later addition
views.holders: Duhm and Cornill, and less firmly Giesebrecht, as reported by the Cambridge Bible (Streane, revised 1913)

argument.text: The Cambridge Bible notes that the verses are “also absent from LXX”, and that Nebuzar-adan, named there, did not come to Jerusalem till a month after the city was taken (Jer 52:6, 12); it reports that Duhm and Cornill reject them, and Giesebrecht “less confidently”. In the Greek (Brenton, chapter 46) verses 4–13 are missing but verse 14 is there.

views.label: Yes
views.holders: The Septuagint's heading; the Talmud (Baba Bathra 15a); C. F. Keil (1874)

argument.text: The Greek opens: “And it came to pass, after Israel was taken captive, and Jerusalem made desolate, that Jeremias sat weeping, and lamented with this lamentation over Jerusalem”. The Talmud: “Jeremiah wrote his book, Kings, and Lamentations.” Keil holds the tradition “is as well-founded as any ancient historical tradition whatever.”

views.label: Probably not; a writer or writers of his time
views.holders: S. R. Driver (1891)

argument.text: Driver: “There is no statement in the OT. as to the authorship of the Lamentations”; the tradition “can be traced back to the LXX”, but “the balance of internal evidence may be said to preponderate against Jeremiah's authorship of the Book.” He adds that the poems are “the work of a contemporary (or contemporaries)”.

notSaid: Scripture does not record Jeremiah's death, his age, or his grave.
The text does not say Jeremiah married; he was told not to take a wife “in this place” (Jer 16:2).
The text says “he cut it with the penknife” after Jehudi read three or four leaves (Jer 36:23); it does not make clear whether “he” is Jehudi or the king. It says the king burned the roll (36:27–28).
At Tophet, at Tahpanhes and with Seraiah's book, the text gives the LORD's or Jeremiah's command and the words to be said, but does not tell the act being done (Jer 19:1–11; 43:8–13; 51:59–64).
Jeremiah of Libnah, father of Hamutal, the mother of Jehoahaz and Zedekiah (2 Kgs 23:31; 24:18), is a different man.
Matthew's “Jeremy” at Matthew 27:9 is discussed below; the words Matthew gives are not found in that form in the book of Jeremiah.

prophets.name: Hananiah
prophets.title: “The LORD hath not sent thee” (Jeremiah 28:15)
prophets.tagline: A prophet from Gibeon who broke Jeremiah's yoke and promised the captives home within two years.

claim.text: He spoke “in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fourth year, and in the fifth month”, in the house of the LORD.
He promised that the LORD would bring back “Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah, with all the captives of Judah, that went into Babylon”.
His word was that the LORD would break “the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the neck of all nations within the space of two full years”.

how.text: He spoke in the LORD's name: “Thus speaketh the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel”. He spoke in the house of the LORD before the priests and all the people.
He acted his word out: he took the yoke off Jeremiah's neck, broke it, and said “Even so will I break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar”.

The Hebrew text, and the King James Version made from it, give him the title “the prophet” six times (Jer 28:1, 5, 10, 12, 15, 17). The Greek Septuagint names him at his first mention “Ananias the false prophet” (Greek chapter 35:1, in Brenton's translation of 1844).

message.theme: The yoke of Babylon is broken

claim.text: Against Jeremiah, who was wearing a yoke to say “serve the king of Babylon”, Hananiah said the yoke was already broken.

quotes.text: Thus speaketh the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, saying, I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon.

claim.text: Within two years the temple vessels, King Jeconiah and all the captives would come back from Babylon.

quotes.text: Within two full years will I bring again into this place all the vessels of the LORD’s house

words.to: All the people, in the temple

quote.text: Even so will I break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the neck of all nations within the space of two full years.

claim.text: “Then Hananiah the prophet took the yoke from off the prophet Jeremiah’s neck, and brake it.”

word.text: Jeremiah first said “Amen: the LORD do so”, and set out a test: the prophet who prophesies peace is known as sent by the LORD “when the word of the prophet shall come to pass”.

reported.text: Scripture does not record the vessels or the captives coming back within two years. The return comes in Ezra, in the first year of Cyrus.

word.text: After the yoke was broken the word came to Jeremiah: “Thou hast broken the yokes of wood; but thou shalt make for them yokes of iron.” Then: “The LORD hath not sent thee … this year thou shalt die, because thou hast taught rebellion against the LORD.”

reported.text: “So Hananiah the prophet died the same year in the seventh month.”

claim.text: Jeremiah answered him in front of the priests and people, then “went his way” until the word of the LORD came.
“Hananiah the son of Azur the prophet, which was of Gibeon”.

places.name: Gibeon
places.note: His home town

places.name: The house of the LORD, Jerusalem
places.note: Where he spoke

scripture.text: He died “the same year in the seventh month”; his own word had been spoken in the fifth month.

notSaid: The text does not say how Hananiah died.
Scripture says nothing of Hananiah before or after this one chapter, and gives no call.
Jeremiah 28:1 dates the meeting “in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah … in the fourth year”, and 27:1 says Jehoiakim; the question is set out on Jeremiah's page.

prophets.name: Ahab
prophets.title: Prophesied “a lie unto you in my name” (Jeremiah 29:21)
prophets.tagline: A prophet among the captives in Babylon, named in Jeremiah's letter with Zedekiah son of Maaseiah.

claim.text: Jeremiah's letter said the LORD would deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar, “and he shall slay them before your eyes”.
The letter naming them went to Babylon by the hand of the men Zedekiah sent to Nebuchadnezzar.

how.text: He was one of the prophets among the captives: the letter answers those who said “The LORD hath raised us up prophets in Babylon”, and warns, “Let not your prophets and your diviners, that be in the midst of you, deceive you”.

message.theme: What he said is not recorded

claim.text: The text does not give his words. It says only that he and his companion prophesied “a lie unto you in my name” and spoke “lying words in my name, which I have not commanded them”.

quotes.text: Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, of Ahab the son of Kolaiah, and of Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, which prophesy a lie unto you in my name

quote.text: Because they have committed villany in Israel, and have committed adultery with their neighbours’ wives, and have spoken lying words in my name, which I have not commanded them; even I know, and am a witness, saith the LORD.

claim.text: Jeremiah's letter, spoken about him and his companion to all the captivity.

word.text: They would be delivered to Nebuchadrezzar and slain before the captives' eyes, and their names would become a curse: “The LORD make thee like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire”.

reported.text: Scripture does not narrate their end. The curse of Jeremiah 29:22 speaks of them as men “whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire”.

claim.text: Named with him in the same sentence and the same judgment.
“Ahab the son of Kolaiah”.
Wrote the letter that names him.

places.name: Babylon
places.note: Among the captives

scripture.text: Foretold: the king of Babylon would slay him before the captives' eyes.

tradition.text: A learned Hebrew told Origen that the two elders in the story of Susanna were the men of Jeremiah 29: “The Lord make you like Zedekias and Achiab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire”. Another Hebrew told him they had deceived the captives' wives by claiming to explain “the things concerning Christ”.
tradition.who: Origen, Letter to Africanus 7–8, reporting what Jewish teachers told him
tradition.when: first half of the 3rd century AD

notSaid: Scripture records nothing else about him: no words of his own, no deeds, no date of death.
The text does not say what lie he prophesied; the letter's surrounding words concern the length of the captivity (Jer 29:8–10, 29:28), but they are not attributed to him.
The phrase “roasted in the fire” is part of the curse foretold in Jeremiah 29:22; no narrative of the event exists in Scripture.

prophets.name: Shemaiah the Nehelamite
prophets.title: “I sent him not” (Jeremiah 29:31)
prophets.tagline: Wrote from Babylon to the priests at Jerusalem asking why Jeremiah had not been reproved.

claim.text: He wrote to Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah, the priest whom Zedekiah sent to Jeremiah, after Jeremiah's letter came to Babylon in Zedekiah's reign.

how.text: He “sent letters in thy name unto all the people that are at Jerusalem, and to Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest, and to all the priests”. The LORD's word says he “hath prophesied unto you”.
Where the Hebrew and the King James Version have “Shemaiah the Nehelamite”, the Greek Septuagint has “Samæas the Ælamite” (Greek chapter 36:24, in Brenton's translation of 1844).

claim.text: He reminded Zephaniah that he had been made priest to put “every man that is mad, and maketh himself a prophet” in prison and the stocks, and asked why Jeremiah had not been reproved for telling the captives the captivity would be long.

quotes.text: Now therefore why hast thou not reproved Jeremiah of Anathoth, which maketh himself a prophet to you?
This captivity is long: build ye houses, and dwell in them

quote.text: Because that Shemaiah hath prophesied unto you, and I sent him not, and he caused you to trust in a lie

word.text: He and his seed would be punished: “he shall not have a man to dwell among this people; neither shall he behold the good that I will do for my people”.

reported.text: Scripture does not record what became of him or his family.

person.name: Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest

claim.text: Shemaiah's letter was sent to him; “Zephaniah the priest read this letter in the ears of Jeremiah the prophet.”
The one Shemaiah wanted restrained; the word about Shemaiah came to Jeremiah.

places.name: Babylon
places.note: He wrote as one of the captives (“he sent unto us in Babylon”)

scripture.text: Foretold: no man of his would dwell among the people, nor would he see the good to come.

notSaid: The text does not explain “Nehelamite”, and no place or family of that name appears elsewhere in Scripture.
Scripture does not say what Zephaniah did after reading the letter to Jeremiah, beyond reading it.
He is a different man from Shemaiah the man of God in Rehoboam's day (1 Kgs 12:22) and Shemaiah in Nehemiah 6:10.

prophets.name: Obadiah
prophets.title: The vision of Obadiah (Obadiah 1)
prophets.tagline: Twenty-one verses against Edom, for standing by when strangers entered Jerusalem's gates.

how.text: The book is called “The vision of Obadiah”, and the words are the LORD's: “Thus saith the Lord GOD concerning Edom; We have heard a rumour from the LORD”.

claim.text: Edom trusted its high rock dwellings; the LORD would bring it down and its allies would turn on it.

quotes.text: The pride of thine heart hath deceived thee, thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock
Though thou exalt thyself as the eagle, and though thou set thy nest among the stars, thence will I bring thee down, saith the LORD.

claim.text: The book charges Edom with standing on the other side on the day strangers carried away Jerusalem's forces and cast lots on the city, and tells Edom it should not have rejoiced, entered the gate, laid hands on the goods or cut off those who escaped.

quotes.text: For thy violence against thy brother Jacob shame shall cover thee, and thou shalt be cut off for ever.

claim.text: The day of the LORD is near upon all nations; Edom's deeds would return on its own head.

quotes.text: as thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee: thy reward shall return upon thine own head.

message.theme: Mount Zion, and the kingdom the LORD's

claim.text: Deliverance and holiness on mount Zion; the house of Jacob would possess the lands around, and the captives come home.

quotes.text: And saviours shall come up on mount Zion to judge the mount of Esau; and the kingdom shall be the LORD’s.

quote.text: Thou shouldest not have entered into the gate of my people in the day of their calamity

claim.text: One chapter of 21 verses, the shortest book of the Old Testament. Verses 1–4 and 5–6 are close in wording to Jeremiah 49:14–16 and 49:9–10, in Jeremiah's words against Edom.

outline.title: The day of the LORD; Zion and the kingdom

places.name: Sepharad
places.note: Where “the captivity of Jerusalem” is; not pinned, as its location is uncertain

scripture.text: Scripture says nothing of this Obadiah beyond the title of his book.

views.label: Under Jehoram of Judah
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1868)

argument.text: Philistines and Arabians broke into Judah in Jehoram's day (2 Chr 21:16–17). Keil: “there only remains the taking of Jerusalem by the Philistines and Arabians in the time of Jehoram”.

views.label: In Amaziah's reign
views.holders: Seder Olam, as reported by the Jewish Encyclopedia (1905)

argument.text: “The prophecy of Obadiah occurred in the time of Amaziah, King of Judah”.

views.label: Early, foretelling the Babylonian capture
views.holders: E. B. Pusey (The Minor Prophets, 1860–77)

argument.text: Pusey reads verses 11–14 as a prediction of Nebuchadnezzar's siege, and holds that since Obadiah came before Jeremiah “it was probably long anterior to it.”

views.label: After the fall of Jerusalem in 586
views.holders: S. R. Driver (1891); G. A. Smith (1898), for verses 10–21

argument.text: Driver: the expressions in verses 11–14 “are most naturally referred to the destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldaeans in 586”. Smith takes verses 10–21 so, but holds that verses 1–9 “probably reflect earlier events”.

questions.question: Who borrowed from whom, Obadiah or Jeremiah 49?

views.label: Jeremiah used Obadiah

argument.text: Keil: “Obadiah did not use Jeremiah, but that Jeremiah read and made use of Obadiah.” Pusey: “Jeremiah reset the words of Obadiah in his own prophecy.”

views.label: Both used an older prophecy
views.holders: S. R. Driver (1891)

argument.text: The common elements came “from a prophecy older than either, which Ob. has incorporated with least alteration, while Jer. has treated it with greater freedom.”

views.label: Obadiah took in an older oracle that Jeremiah had also used
views.holders: G. A. Smith (1898)

argument.text: Smith holds that the author began “by incorporating in vv. 1-6 a pre-exilic prophecy against Edom, which had been already, and with more freedom, used by Jeremiah.”

notSaid: Scripture gives no father, home, king or date for Obadiah.
The text does not say whether he is any of the other men named Obadiah, such as Ahab's steward (1 Kgs 18:3).
The book does not name the strangers who entered Jerusalem's gates (Obad 11); which attack is meant is the question of its date.
The New Testament does not quote Obadiah.

prophets.name: Nahum
prophets.title: Nahum the Elkoshite (Nahum 1:1)
prophets.tagline: “The burden of Nineveh”: the LORD's judgment on the bloody city, and good tidings for Judah.

how.text: The book calls itself both “The burden of Nineveh” and “The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite”.

message.theme: The LORD who is slow to anger, and avenges

claim.text: The book opens with who the LORD is: jealous, avenging, slow to anger, great in power, and good to those who trust him.

quotes.text: The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked
The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him.

claim.text: The yoke would be broken from Judah's neck; Judah is told to keep its feasts.

quotes.text: Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace!

claim.text: The attack is pictured: red shields, raging chariots, the gates of the rivers opened, the palace dissolved, the spoil taken; the lions' den emptied.

quotes.text: Woe to the bloody city! it is all full of lies and robbery
Nineveh is laid waste: who will bemoan her?

claim.text: Nineveh is asked whether it is better than “populous No”, which had rivers round it and Ethiopia and Egypt for strength, “Yet was she carried away”.

quote.text: Behold, I am against thee, saith the LORD of hosts
O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows: for the wicked shall no more pass through thee
Thy shepherds slumber, O king of Assyria: thy nobles shall dwell in the dust

claim.text: Three chapters, 47 verses, all against Nineveh except the words of comfort to Judah. It names no king of Judah and no year.

outline.title: The LORD who avenges; comfort for Judah
The siege and fall of the city

places.name: Elkosh
places.note: Not pinned: where it was is not known (see the question); the atlas's point in Galilee follows one tradition

places.name: No (Thebes)
places.note: “Populous No”; the atlas places it at Thebes

scripture.text: Scripture says nothing of Nahum outside the first verse of his book.

tradition.text: A grave at Alkush (Alqosh), near Mosul, “is shown as that of Nahum”.
tradition.who: A local tradition near Mosul, reported by S. R. Driver (1891)
tradition.when: Driver: it “cannot be traced back beyond the 16th cent.”

views.label: Between the fall of Thebes and the fall of Nineveh
views.holders: S. R. Driver (1891); A. B. Davidson (1896); G. A. Smith (1898)

argument.text: Nahum 3:8–10 speaks of No as already carried away. Driver takes No to be Thebes, captured by Ashurbanipal “shortly after 664”, and the latest limit to be Nineveh's fall, which he and Davidson dated about 607–606. Driver: “Within these limits it is impossible to fix the date more precisely.”

views.label: Soon after Sennacherib's defeat, under Hezekiah
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1868), following Vitringa

argument.text: Keil quotes Vitringa: “the date of Nahum must be fixed a very short time after Isaiah and Micah, and therefore in the reign of Hezekiah”.

views.label: In Manasseh's reign
views.holders: Seder Olam, a Jewish chronology ascribed by Jewish authorities to Rabbi Jose ben Halafta, as reported by the Jewish Encyclopedia (1905)

argument.text: It places “those of Joel, Nahum, and Habakkuk in the reign of Manasseh.”

questions.question: What do the records outside the Bible say of Thebes and Nineveh?

views.label: Ashurbanipal's annals on Thebes
views.holders: Rassam Cylinder, translated by D. D. Luckenbill (1927)

argument.text: Ashurbanipal says of Ni', which Luckenbill renders Thebes: “That city (i.e., Ni') my hands captured in its entirety, — with the aid of Assur and Ishtar.” The annals do not name Nahum or Judah here.

views.label: A Babylonian chronicle on Nineveh
views.holders: British Museum tablet 21,901, published by C. J. Gadd (1923)

argument.text: The chronicle tells of the king of Akkad mustering his army in his fourteenth year and of the city taken and turned “into a mound and a ru[in]”. Gadd: the date is “now securely placed in the month of Ab (i.e. July—August), of the year B.C. 612.” Scholars before 1923, Driver and Davidson among them, put the fall about 607–606.

views.label: A village in Galilee
views.holders: Jerome (about AD 400), in the preface to his commentary on Nahum, quoted by Davidson (1896)

argument.text: “Helkesei is still at this day a hamlet in Galilee, small indeed, and scarcely shewing traces by ruins of ancient buildings, but for all that known to the Jews, and pointed out to me by a guide.”

views.label: In the south, of the tribe of Simeon
views.holders: The Lives of the Prophets ascribed to Epiphanius, as reported by Davidson (1896)

argument.text: In the Syriac copy: “Nahum was of Elkosh, beyond Bet Gabre, of the tribe of Simeon.” Davidson notes the work is “usually ascribed, though perhaps wrongly, to Epiphanius”.

views.label: Alqosh near Mosul
views.holders: A local tradition, reported by Driver (1891)

argument.text: A place called Alkush near Mosul shows a grave as Nahum's, “but the tradition connecting this locality with the prophet cannot be traced back beyond the 16th cent.” Davidson's verdict on all three: “These conflicting traditions leave the prophet's birthplace quite uncertain.”

notSaid: Scripture gives no call, no king and no date for Nahum, and nothing of his life.
Scripture does not record the fall of Nineveh.
The New Testament does not quote Nahum. Romans 10:15's “How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace” is closest in wording to Isaiah 52:7; Nahum 1:15 has a similar line.

prophets.name: Habakkuk
prophets.title: Habakkuk the prophet (Habakkuk 1:1)
prophets.tagline: He asked the LORD “how long?”, waited on his watch for the answer, and ended in a song.

how.text: “The burden which Habakkuk the prophet did see.” Much of the book is his own questions to the LORD and the LORD's answers.
He waited for the answer like a watchman: “I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower”. He was told to write the vision down plainly “upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.”
Chapter 3 is “A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet upon Shigionoth”, with “Selah” in it and a note at the end for “the chief singer on my stringed instruments”.

claim.text: He complains that violence and wrong judgment go unpunished.

quotes.text: O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!

claim.text: The answer: a work “which ye will not believe”, the Chaldeans, “that bitter and hasty nation”.

quotes.text: For, lo, I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation

message.theme: Why the wicked over the righteous?

claim.text: His second question: how can the LORD, “of purer eyes than to behold evil”, let the wicked devour the man more righteous than he?

message.theme: The just shall live by his faith

claim.text: The vision will come at its time; the proud man is not upright, “but the just shall live by his faith.” The New Testament quotes it three times (see The book).

quotes.text: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry.
but the just shall live by his faith.

claim.text: Woes on the plunderer, on him who builds his house by evil gain, on him who builds a town with blood, on him who makes his neighbour drunk, and on the maker of idols; then silence before the LORD.

quotes.text: For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea.
But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him.

claim.text: His prayer recalls the LORD coming from Teman and Paran, and ends in trust though every harvest fails.

quotes.text: Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines
Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation.

quote.text: Because thou hast spoiled many nations, all the remnant of the people shall spoil thee

claim.text: Three chapters, 56 verses: two complaints and two answers, five woes, and a prayer set for singing. It names the Chaldeans but no king and no year.

outline.title: The vision; the just shall live by faith; five woes

quotedInNT.note: Paul at Antioch in Pisidia, after the warning about what “is spoken of in the prophets” (Acts 13:40). Its “ye despisers” follows the Greek of Habakkuk 1:5 (“Behold, ye despisers”, Brenton 1844), where the King James Old Testament has “among the heathen”.
“As it is written, The just shall live by faith.”

“Will not tarry … the just shall live by faith”. Its words “if any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him” follow the Greek of Habakkuk 2:4 (“If he should draw back, my soul has no pleasure in him”, Brenton 1844), not the Hebrew.

places.name: Teman
places.note: Named in his prayer: “God came from Teman”

places.name: Mount Paran
places.note: Named in his prayer

scripture.text: Scripture says nothing of Habakkuk outside his book.

tradition.text: An angel carries “a prophet, called Habbacuc” by the hair of his head from Judea to Babylon to bring Daniel his dinner in the lions' den, and sets him back again. T. Witton Davies judged this episode a later addition to the story.
tradition.who: Bel and the Dragon 33–39, an addition to Daniel in the Greek Bible, printed in the Apocrypha of the King James Version
tradition.when: Davies (1913) assumes a Hebrew text of about 136 BC, the Greek being later

tradition.text: The Greek heading of Bel and the Dragon says it was taken “From the prophecy of Hambakoum, son of Jesus, of the tribe of Levi.”
tradition.who: The Septuagint's heading to Bel and the Dragon, as translated by A. B. Davidson (1896)
tradition.when: In the Greek translation, which Davies (1913) holds later than a Hebrew original; no firmer date is given here

tradition.text: Habakkuk was of the tribe of Simeon. “It is said that when Jerusalem fell in 586 he fled to Ostracine on the borders of Egypt, but returned to his native place on the withdrawal of the Chaldeans … and died two years before the return of the exiles from Babylon. His tomb was pointed out in Keilah.”
tradition.who: The Lives of the Prophets ascribed to Epiphanius, as summarised by A. B. Davidson (1896)
tradition.when: Davidson calls the ascription to Epiphanius (bishop from AD 367) perhaps wrong; he does not date the work

views.label: Under Jehoiakim, as the Chaldeans rose
views.holders: S. R. Driver (1891); A. B. Davidson (1896)

argument.text: The Chaldeans are being raised up (Hab 1:6). Driver: “The prophecy may be assigned with great probability to the reign of Jehoiakim (B.C. 608-598)”. Davidson puts chapter 1:5–11 no earlier than the battle of Carchemish (“605 — 4”).

views.label: Late in Manasseh's reign
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1868); Seder Olam, as reported by the Jewish Encyclopedia (1905)

argument.text: Keil narrows the choice to Josiah's reign or “the closing years of Manasseh” and leans to Manasseh. The Seder Olam places Joel, Nahum and Habakkuk “in the reign of Manasseh.”

notSaid: Scripture gives no call, no family, no home and no king for Habakkuk.
Habakkuk 3 is set for music, but the text does not say Habakkuk was a Levite or a temple singer.
